Use air as the working fluid with specific-heat ratio γ = 1.4 and specific gas constant R = 287 J/(kg·K), as agreed.

Recognize that the Rayleigh-Pitot formula applies only to supersonic flow with a detached shock standing in front of a Pitot tube, so it is not valid at M = 0.5; use the standard isentropic compression relations (Saint-Venant–Wantzel relations for a Pitot tube in subsonic flow) instead.

Apply the isentropic relations at the incoming Mach number M = 0.5 to compute the stagnation-to-static ratios T₀/T = 1 + (γ−1)/2 · M², p₀/p = (1 + (γ−1)/2 · M²)^(γ/(γ−1)), and ρ₀/ρ = (1 + (γ−1)/2 · M²)^(1/(γ−1)).

Adopt standard sea-level static reference conditions of p = 101,325 Pa and T = 288.15 K for the absolute-value numerical example.

Derive the supporting static quantities from those reference conditions: static density ρ = p/(RT), static speed of sound a = √(γRT), and flow velocity V = M·a.

Compute the absolute stagnation quantities: stagnation pressure p₀ = (p₀/p)·p, stagnation temperature T₀ = (T₀/T)·T, stagnation density ρ₀ = (ρ₀/ρ)·ρ, and stagnation speed of sound a₀ = √(γRT₀).

Present all stagnation-to-static ratios with 4 to 5 significant figures and all absolute values with a consistent precision throughout, using SI units (Pa, K, kg/m³, m/s).

Organize the final output into a short summary table that consolidates the stagnation-to-static ratios, the absolute stagnation quantities, and the supporting static quantities for quick reference.

Include a brief opening note explaining that the isentropic relations are used in place of the Rayleigh-Pitot formula because the flow at M = 0.5 is subsonic and no detached shock stands in front of the Pitot probe.
